newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Funds see no sustained Korean recovery.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Funds see no sustained Korean recovery.

text.p: Poor economic fundamentals will soon renew pressure on South Korean shares despite an immediate recovery from a badly oversold position late last year, Asian fund managers said on Wednesday.
A rush of foreign funds was partly credited with further strength in the KOSPI on Wednesday following the previous session's 4.1 percent rise to 686.59 points.
The gains came despite calls for an all-out strike on Tuesday from South Korea's largest union to protest against new labour laws.
The composite index was up 3.56 points or 0.52 percent at 690.15 points at midday on Wednesday.
While the market welcomed the weak response to the strike call, continuing labour unrest will depress further strength and a slide back to the low 600s was likely, fund managers said.

"In the long term, Korea must be a good buying opportunity but in the short term, it may be worth our while to wait for a clearer solution to the labour situation," said Stephen Leung, chief investment officer at BZW Asia.

Matthew Choi, Korean fund manager at Thornton Management (Asia) Ltd, said the trade picture will have to improve substantially in the second half of the year for South Korean shares to make a sustained recovery.
"That means better DRAM (dynamic random access memory) prices or a pick-up in world trade," he said.
Memory chip exports make up 30 percent of South Korea's electronics exports, which in turn account for 21 percent of the country's overall exports.
Fund managers said the KOSPI reached a critical point at 650 points on January 3, when a margin call forced out domestic investors, creating a buying opportunity for foreign investors.
"Margin loans exceeded three trillion won (US$3.53 billion) and created some panic selling to close down positions," one fund manager said.
"For the foreigners this was a good opportunity. The index kept hitting 600 and coming back even though the strike situation keeps on getting worse."
But analysts said South Korea, which continues to restrict foreign investment to 20 percent of share capital, offers few fundamental reasons for the recent enthusiasm.

Its current account deficit is among the worst in Asia, nearing five percent of gross domestic product, while a regional slump in exports was exacerbated by the won's failure to depreciate in line with the yen, reducing South Korea's competitiveness still further in key markets.
The won has also failed to benefit much from the recent strengthening of the U.S. dollar.

But there are a couple of promising signs, said Graham Courtney, director of Asian economics for SBC Warburg. The central bank has kept money supply more accommodative than the recent slight decline in interest rates suggests, he said.

In addition to a benchmark bond yield of 12.5 percent in a stable inflationary environment of about 4.8 percent, the central bank allowed M2 growth of about 20 percent as soon as the exports slump hit early last year, well above targeted levels of 15.5 percent, Courtney said.
"That suggests the Bank of Korea has been making more money available through the banking system to accommodate the need for working capital," he said.
This has reduced the cost of working capital for some of the nation's largest corporations, burdened by heavy inventories which will fall due to the labour unrest, Courtney added.
"The central bank has been providing a monetary backdrop that has been accommodative enough to encourage companies to deal with inventories of their own accord," he said.
"The enforced cutback of production is the best thing that could happen in Korea right now."
While the short-term outlook remains gloomy, foreign investors said South Korea could offer good longer term returns.
"Resistance to change and the entrenched bureaucracy will make it very difficult. However, long term, the outlook could be good," said Mark Mobius at Templeton International.
